name: PT Ulima Nitra Tbk

frontmatter.title: Ulima Nitra: a sustained fleet and a receivable the market will not pay for
frontmatter.summary: Ulima Nitra is a South Sumatran contract miner that strips overburden and hauls coal for four mine owners, owns no concession and earns a fee, not a coal price. We reiterate at BUY on a research-only basis with a Rp176 value against a Rp137 price. Capex now funds a sustaining fleet rather than a harvest, and the value rests on collecting the receivable.
thesis: This is a fee business, not a coal producer: mining services and equipment rental were almost all of FY2024 net sales [S4 p.53, F13, F15], there is no coal-sales line, no concession and no royalty in the cost notes, so we model it on the contractor template and refuse the commodity-producer price link.

The quota is the revenue line. The ministry cut the 2026 production plan below the volume produced in 2025 and late RKAB approvals took the first quarter out from under the company [S8, S9]; the second quarter was back near the FY2025 quarterly average, and FY2027E holds that exit run-rate, for IDR569.2bn of revenue [S0, S5 p.6].

The fleet has to be paid for. The property and equipment note leaves only part of gross cost undepreciated [S5 p.36, F41, F42], so capex is now set equal to the depreciation charge and net property and equipment holds at IDR390.4bn instead of collapsing; that correction alone takes the discounted cash flow from the last version's figure to Rp159 a share [S5 p.36, F8].

Earnings quality is the risk, not leverage: receivables of IDR330.0bn gross at the end of the first quarter, of which IDR197.5bn is more than three months overdue and IDR150.3bn is one client whose contract expired [S5 p.33, F19, F34, F35].

The Rp176 value is 30.0% above the price, but the name fails the house investability floors on market capitalisation and traded value [S0]; the rating is a research-only valuation observation for the desk, not a trade recommendation.

Audited FY2026 accounts, any FY2026 dividend, and the Banyan receivable balance

blocks.text: UNIQ strips overburden and hauls coal for four mine owners in South Sumatra, rents heavy equipment to them, and owns no concession [S2, S4 p.53]. We reiterate at BUY on a research-only basis with a Rp176 twelve-month value, 30.0% above the Rp137 price, on a discounted cash flow at 80% of the valuation weight [S2, S4 p.41].

Three things changed, and two of them go against the call. First, capex is now set equal to the depreciation charge in every forecast year. The last version spent at the recent observed rate and added back a depreciation charge a third larger, which took net property and equipment from IDR390.4bn to a fraction of that by the end of the decade and left the terminal value harvesting a fleet that no longer existed; the property and equipment note leaves only part of gross cost undepreciated, so a contractor earning revenue to the middle of the next decade has to replace it [S5 p.36, F41, F42]. On a sustaining fleet the discounted cash flow is Rp159 a share and free cash flow falls accordingly. Second, the peer cross-checks carry a tenth of the weight each instead of a quarter and a sixth, because the peer median moved a quarter in two days when the September quarter rolled into the trailing windows while UNIQ's own earnings did not move [S0]. Third, the receivable is now valued on both sides: the cash flow holds the book at cost and never releases it, so the bridge credits an expected recovery of the stalled Banyan balance instead of deducting an impairment against an asset that earns nothing [S5 p.33, F19]. The net of the three is a target below the last version's, on the same view of the quota and the contract register [S0, S4, S5].

The gap is what the price already assumes. At Rp137 the market capitalisation plus the FY2025A balance-sheet net debt of IDR156.1bn is 3.4x times last year's EBITDA of IDR174.8bn, and the equity trades at 0.9x book, which is a harvest multiple on a family-controlled register with a 10.9% float [S0]. An explicit contraction test does not confirm that a permanent contraction is priced: a no-recovery path and even a flat-revenue path stay above the market price, and only a decade of shrinking revenue every single year reaches it (section four) [S0, S9].

Four things move the value. The national quota, because the ministry cut the 2026 production plan below the volume produced in 2025 and late RKAB approvals took the first quarter's revenue out from under the company [S8, S9]. The contract register, because Banyan's contract expired in May 2025 and the Budi Gema Gempita extension lapsed into renewal while that client is 45.7% of first-quarter revenue [S4 p.63, S5 p.48, F30]. The receivable, because IDR197.5bn of the IDR330.0bn gross book is more than three months overdue and the allowance against it is a fraction of that [S5 p.33, F34, F35]. And the fleet, where the sustaining capex now in the base case is the largest single change to the cash flow [S5 p.36, F8, F41].

The BUY is a research-only valuation observation, not an actionable position. A market capitalisation of IDR430.0bn, an average daily traded value of IDR1.4bn and a free float of 10.9% all sit below the house investability floors, and the engine returns the name as not investable [S0].

PT Ulima Nitra Tbk began in 1992 as a heavy-equipment rental contractor and moved into coal mining services in 2008, which became its main line by 2010; it listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in March 2021 and has 3,139m shares in issue, unchanged since then [S2 p.43, S5 p.5]. The company operates almost entirely in South Sumatra, and the financial statements are those of the Company alone, with no consolidated subsidiaries and no minority interest [S2 p.43, S4 p.5].

FY2024 net sales of IDR670.1bn split into mining services of IDR602.3bn, vehicle and heavy equipment rental of IDR52.4bn, and smaller construction and other lines, so the fee-for-rock business is almost nine tenths of revenue and rental is most of the rest [S4 p.53, F13, F15]. The segment cost lines carry the same split, with mining services absorbing the fleet, the fuel and the wages, and the rental line carrying a thinner share of depreciation [S4 p.54]. The mix moved sharply in FY2024: construction services fell by more than four fifths and rental by a quarter, while mining services grew by a third, which is the company choosing contract mining over ancillary work [S4 p.53].

The customer register is concentrated, and unlike a producer's reserve it has to be re-won. Four customers were 88.5% of FY2024 net sales, the largest just under half, and PT Banyan Koalindo Lestari was 18.4% in FY2024 [S4 p.53, F16, F17]. The contract register in the Q1 2026 filing is explicit about terms. The Banyan (BKL) contract No. 010/PJ-BKL-UN/2019 dated 29 May 2019 was amended to run to 26 May 2025 or a fixed overburden volume, and it has not been renewed: Banyan was 0.1% of Q1 2026 revenue against 18.4% in FY2024 [S4 p.63, S5 p.48, F29]. The BGG agreement No. 2/BGG-UN/2022 began on 1 February 2022 for one year and was extended on 1 February 2023 for three years, so its term ran to about 1 February 2026; the filing says the contract is currently in renewal process [S5 p.59]. Duta Energy Minerama's contract is suspended pending land release, and Duta Bara Utama's mining and rental contracts were amended most recently on 5 August 2025 on a three-year term [S5 p.58-59]. The ten-year mining-service contract recorded in the Q1 2026 filing (No. 001/PKS BB/DUE-UNT/X/2023, dated 9 October 2023, for the Wiraduta mine) and the Medco heavy-equipment rentals signed in 2025 are the long-dated part of the book [S5 p.59-60]. At the end of the first quarter the mix was BGG at 45.7%, Wiraduta at 17.6%, Medco Grissik at 14.1% and Duta Bara Utama at 11.0%, with Banyan at 0.1% [S5 p.48, F29-F33]. No sales were made to related parties, so the customer concentration is external concentration rather than family self-dealing [S4 p.53, S4 p.61].

Operations are measured in overburden and coal. The company removed 15.1 million bcm of overburden and produced 3.9 Mt of coal in FY2024, both records, with the coal volume up by more than two fifths on FY2023 [S2 p.25, F11, F12]. Physical availability of the loading fleet held at the prior year's level while hauler availability fell, which management attributes to haul units still awaiting renewal, and the company runs stretch-life maintenance rather than a replacement programme [S2 p.44]. It employs 1,008 people [S0].

Revenue is earned as a rate per cubic metre moved and per tonne hauled, agreed with the mine owner inside an annual mine plan, so the company takes volume risk on the client's quota and rate risk at the annual reset, but not coal price risk on its own book [S4 p.53-54]. It pays no royalty, because it holds no licence: the cost-of-sales note carries fuel, salaries, depreciation, repairs, field costs, consumption, safety, insurance, transport and a penalty line, and no royalty or dead-rent item at all [S4 p.53-54]. The service contracts sit with clients who hold the mining licence, and the company also runs join operations on client mines in South Sumatra [S2 p.43].

Management's stated strategy is to keep bidding for mining services in coal and non-coal minerals, for mine works and for secondary mining support, rather than to buy reserves [S2 p.82]. That is a fee-business strategy and it is the reason we model the company on the contractor template rather than as a coal producer, which is set out under section four.

The industry code needs a word. The data pack carries UNIQ as COAL, but that is the provisional exchange fallback: the sub-industry recorded for the name is oil, gas and coal services and equipment, and the house classification file maps exactly that string to mining contractors [S2 p.43, S4 p.53]. A commodity-producer build would tie revenue to a coal price the company does not sell at and apply a royalty schedule to service revenue the company does not pay, which is what the cost notes prove [S4 p.53-54]. The packet needs a forward classification row from the Sector Lead so a re-resolution does not send the name back to COAL; configuration is not ours to edit.

Indonesia is the swing thermal-coal supplier of the region. The company's own annual report records a record national production year in 2024, of which just over half was exported, against a lower total in 2023 [S2]. The Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources then reports production easing in 2025 on weaker demand from China and India and stronger domestic demand from power stations and smelters [S9].

The direction of policy for 2026 is contraction. The minister has said national output will be set below the volume actually produced in 2025, framed as matching domestic need and protecting reserves rather than maximising volume [S9]. Every contract miner's revenue is downstream of that number, because the company mines what its clients' quotas allow and nothing else [S9, S4 p.53].

The instrument is the RKAB, the work plan and budget approved by the ministry for each licence holder. The ministry describes the RKAB as a production-control instrument rather than an administrative step, and the miners' association says late and cut 2026 approvals left licence holders' production allocations uncertain, disrupted domestic supply obligations and pushed the sector to ask that approvals be finished before the year starts [S8]. That is the direct cause of the company's first-quarter revenue collapse: its clients could not mine to plan [S8, S5 p.6].

Prices matter through the client, and the house deck expects the tailwind to fade. The reference prices for the lower-calorific grades that South Sumatran mines produce rose into November 2026 while the high-calorific benchmark fell, and it is the lower-calorific marker that prices this client base [S10]. But the house coal deck carries the high-calorific benchmark at US$118/t for FY2027E against a US$150/t spot, and the low-calorific marker at US$52.5/t against US$65.1/t, so the deck expects both to fall toward through-cycle [S0]. The client margin a rate reset depends on is therefore a fading tailwind, not a new baseline, which is why the base case holds the gross margin at the FY2025 level from FY2027E rather than at the strong second quarter [S10, S5 p.6]. The market price the think tank cites is well above the domestic obligation price, which the ministry has held fixed since 2018 and which the association complains is now far below the export netback after blending costs [S8, S11]. A higher flat price makes clients want to mine more; the quota decides whether they can.

Fiscal policy is the next variable. The government is preparing a progressive export duty on coal to capture part of the windfall, and the think tank proposing it puts the potential revenue in the tens of trillions of rupiah a year on an assumption that most output is exported [S11]. For a contractor the duty matters second-hand, through the margin its clients earn on each tonne and therefore through their willingness to commission overburden removal, and directly if clients use it to renegotiate rates at the annual reset [S11, S4 p.53].

The competitive landscape is two-tier. The listed comparables we value against are the contract miners with live multiples, DOID, MYOH, IATA, RMKO and DEWA, plus the producers whose mine plans and RKAB quotas set contractor volumes and rates, PTBA, ITMG, BSSR, ADRO and BYAN [S0]. Below them sits a long tail of regional contractors competing for the mine plans of South Sumatran licence holders, of which UNIQ is one [S2 p.43]. Entry needs capital for a fleet of haulers and loaders, a maintenance organisation, a safety record and a local relationship with the licence holder; it does not need a reserve, which is why the number of bidders is large and rates are set by tender [S2 p.44].

The large national contract miners earn fees per cubic metre of overburden and per tonne of coal, carry
producer-sized balance sheets, and have expanded abroad to escape the domestic quota cycle. The regional
tail is mostly family-controlled, competes on rate and on equipment availability rather than technology,
and is the segment this company sits in.

The five forces are unfavourable on the client side and only mildly favourable on the supply side. Buyer power is high: four clients are almost nine tenths of revenue and the largest is close to half [S4 p.53, F16]. Supplier power is moderate, since fuel and tyres are commodity inputs, but the consumer-financing houses that fund the fleet have real leverage over a company this size [S5 p.5]. Substitutes are weak in the short run, because a mine owner either removes the overburden or stops mining, but the owner can insource with its own fleet. New entry is easy at the small end and hard at the large end, which is where the margin is. Rivalry is intense, because the same regional contractors bid the same mine plans every year [S2 p.44].

The investment conclusion from the industry work is that UNIQ's revenue is a quota variable and its margin is a rate-reset variable, and neither is set by the coal price. That is why the model runs revenue growth and gross margin off the company's own contract arithmetic, with Brent carried only as a small fuel cost link, rather than off a Newcastle or HBA forecast [S4 p.53, S10].

The three-year record is a cycle in miniature. Net sales went from IDR571.5bn in FY2023 to IDR670.1bn in FY2024, with the gross margin rising from 15.5% to 19.6% as the higher-margin mining mix and the overburden record came through [S4 p.12, F1, F2, F3, F4], then fell back to IDR572.7bn of revenue and a 17.7% margin in FY2025 as volumes normalised and costs stayed put [S0]. Operating profit peaked at IDR106.4bn in FY2024 and net profit at IDR67.6bn [S4 p.12, F5]. The FY2025 audited financial statements are not posted on the company's IR site: the finance page carries the Q1 2026 filing and the 2024 annual statements, and the 2025 annual report is not published. FY2025 revenue, cost of sales and net profit are therefore the data pack's figures [S0] - labelled as such, not quoted from a filing - while FY2025 depreciation and capex come from the Q1 2026 filing's property-and-equipment note [S5 p.36, F8, F10].

The cost structure explains the operating leverage. Cost of sales of IDR538.8bn in FY2024 split into fuel of IDR149.7bn, salaries of IDR127.3bn, depreciation of IDR107.1bn, repairs and maintenance, field costs and smaller lines for consumption, safety, insurance, transport and penalties [S4 p.53-54, F3, F23, F24]. Fuel and salaries together are just over half of cost of sales and both are largely fixed per operating hour, so a quarter without volume is a quarter without gross profit: Q1 2026 revenue of IDR57.2bn produced a negative gross margin [S5 p.6, F21], and Q2 2026, with revenue back near the FY2025 quarterly average, produced a strongly positive one; the Q2 figure is a data-pack estimate, because the last filed quarter is Q1 2026 [S0].

Depreciation is the largest accounting judgement in the accounts and the one place where the data pack is unusable as supplied. The company charged IDR107.1bn of depreciation in FY2024 and IDR109.6bn in FY2025, more than a fifth of the latter year's cost of sales, and the property and equipment note shows a fleet more than half depreciated against gross cost at the end of FY2025, so it is past mid-life on a book basis [S5 p.36, F6, F8]. The data pack's depreciation line is only the small operating-expense slice, and we restate it from the notes in every year [S5 p.36].

The same restatement applies to capex. Property and equipment additions were IDR87.8bn in FY2024 and IDR63.9bn in FY2025, against a depreciation charge that ran at more than one and a half times that in both years, and against cash purchases in the cash-flow statement of only a fraction of the total because most units are bought under consumer financing [S4 p.14, S5 p.36, F8, F9, F10].

That gap is the reason for the largest change in this version. At the end of FY2025 the fleet stood at IDR996.5bn of gross cost less IDR606.0bn of accumulated depreciation, so most of the asset is written off and roughly three and a half years of charge remains at the current rate, inside an average depreciable life of about eight and a half years [S5 p.36, F41, F42, F8]. A company earning revenue to the middle of the next decade must replace that fleet, so capex is set equal to the charge from FY2026E, at 21.0% of revenue falling to 19.0%, and the terminal year spends what it charges [S5 p.36, F8]. Net property and equipment therefore holds at IDR390.4bn through the forecast instead of falling to a fraction of it, and the EBITDA add-back is backed by a real asset base. The cost is a lower cash flow: free cash flow to the firm is IDR44.2bn in FY2026E and IDR66.5bn in FY2028E, not the near-hundred-billion figures of the last version [S5 p.36]. The physical reason to believe the fleet is being worked hard rather than renewed is in the operating data: hauler availability was 74.2% against loader availability of 80.5% in FY2024, because haul units were awaiting replacement under a stretch-life programme [S2 p.72, F43, F44].

Working capital is where the cash went, and the aging is now disclosed. Trade receivables were IDR330.0bn gross and IDR312.0bn net at 31 March 2026 against FY2025 revenue of IDR572.7bn, which is more than half a year of sales outstanding [S5 p.33, F18, F35]. Of the gross book, IDR197.5bn was more than three months overdue, up from IDR110.6bn three months earlier, and the expected-credit-loss allowance is IDR17.9bn, a small fraction of the overdue balance [S5 p.33, F28, F34, F40]. The concentration mirrors the revenue concentration: Banyan owed IDR150.3bn at the end of March, down from IDR157.1bn at the end of 2025 and IDR80.3bn a year before, so the balance nearly doubled after the contract expired on 26 May 2025 and has since been paid down slightly [S5 p.33, S4 p.38, S4 p.63, F19, F36, F37]. BGG owed IDR79.9bn and Duta Bara Utama IDR63.5bn [S5 p.33, F38, F39]. On the overdue bucket the answer to the obvious question is yes: Banyan paid something after May 2025, and the first quarter of 2026 reduced the balance rather than adding to it [S5 p.33, F19, F36]. We hold operating working capital at the June 2026 actual in FY2026E, so there is no assumed release of the stalled balance in the base cash flow; the collection is credited in the valuation bridge instead (section four).

Debt has come down steadily and is now short-dated. Net debt fell from IDR253.2bn at the end of FY2023 to IDR156.1bn at the end of FY2025, and the June quarter shows a further large repayment [S0]. At the end of March the stack was IDR55.3bn of short-term bank loans, long-term bank debt at a fixed rate in the high sevens, and consumer-financing payables secured on the units themselves at rates running into the low teens, with the bulk of the repayments falling due in 2027 and 2028 [S5 p.5, S5 p.37-38]. Net debt to EBITDA was 0.9 at the end of FY2025, so the leverage is not the problem; the refinancing calendar is [S5 p.5, F26].

Our forecast anchors FY2026E to the actual first half and a second half at the first half's average quarterly rate. Revenue of IDR497.1bn is -13.2% against FY2025, the first quarter's hole that the rest of the year cannot recover, and the gross margin of 19.2% at the live Brent input cost (20.0% at the base input cost) requires the second half to earn roughly the second quarter's actual rate, several points above the second half of last year at a similar revenue level [S5 p.6, S0]. The bridge is explicit: the first half contributed the first quarter's IDR57.2bn of revenue plus a run-rate second quarter, the full year carries IDR95.3bn of gross profit, so the second half carries most of it [S0, S5 p.6, F21]. We anchor on the second quarter because it is the last observed quarter at run-rate revenue and because the fixed quarterly depreciation of IDR26.5bn and the salary line now sit on a normal revenue base; the gross-margin axis of the sensitivity grid prices each point of miss [S5 p.36, F22]. EBITDA of IDR164.9bn is a little below FY2025's IDR174.8bn, while the EBITDA margin rises from 30.5% to 33.2%: the driver is depreciation on a smaller revenue base, not a cash-margin expansion. FY2027E grows revenue by 14.5%, which holds the FY2026E exit run-rate rather than assuming a step-down, and sits below the annualised second quarter, because the second half is the weaker half of that exit level [S0, S5 p.6]. The long run is 4.0% nominal, flat in real terms [S9].

Two earnings-quality flags survive the restatement. The first is the divergence between profit and cash: free cash flow to the firm was IDR21.1bn in FY2025 on a IDR68.1bn working-capital build, which is the receivable rather than the trading, and profit has outrun operating cash in each of the last two years [S0, F18]. The second is the accrual on the fleet: depreciation exceeds capex in every historical year, which flatters reported profit and defers the replacement decision to whoever owns the equity after us [S5 p.36, F8, F10]. That is corrected in the forecast rather than in the narrative. Related-party purchases were 2.7% of net sales in FY2024, up from about one per cent in FY2023, from companies under the same management rather than from the controlling shareholder [S4 p.54, S4 p.61, F27].

The forecast no longer turns net cash inside the explicit decade on the old timing. Net debt falls to IDR106.6bn in FY2027E and IDR22.2bn in FY2029E, with the first net cash year in FY2030E at IDR-13.0bn, and the dividend yield at our modelled distribution is 1.6% on the current price [S0, S5 p.5]. A special dividend or buyback is bull-case optionality, not base-case income.

The method set follows the industry map for mining contractors: a life-of-contract free cash flow to the firm at 80%, an EV/EBITDA cross-check at 10% and a P/E cross-check at 10% [S4 p.41, S5 p.36]. The DCF is primary because the value of a contractor is the fee stream on a finite fleet, not a perpetuity on a reserve. The cross-check weights are deliberately small. The peer median EV/EBITDA fell by a quarter in two days as the September quarter entered the peers' trailing windows, with ADRO and MYOH both roughly halving their trailing EBITDA multiples, while UNIQ's own FY2025A EBITDA was unchanged; IATA's P/E jumped on collapsing peer earnings [S0]. A median whose denominator moves that fast is a cross-check, not a valuation input, and giving it a quarter of the weight cut the last version's target by an eighth with no change in the company's own cash flow. At a tenth each the multiples are still reported, and a window roll can no longer move the call [S0].

The cost of capital is built bottom-up, and the published arithmetic now reproduces its own output. The engine takes the risk-free rate of 7.4%, subtracts the sovereign default spread of 1.6%, and adds the industry beta geared to 1.23 at a debt-to-equity of 0.29 multiplied by the mature-market premium of 4.2% plus the country risk premium of 2.5%, plus a 2.0% premium that aligns the debt leg with the rate the company pays, 9.4% [S5 p.37-38]. That gives a cost of equity of 16.0% and a WACC of 14.1%. Two conventions should be stated: the default-spread term is a real reduction for a rupiah investor who can hold the sovereign instead, and the gearing uses the statutory 22.0% rate for the tax shield while the cash-flow tax rate is the 16.4% the accounts actually show being paid [S4 p.12]. The discounts are 77.5% equity and 22.5% debt.

The DCF produces Rp159 a share, an enterprise value of IDR511.8bn with the terminal value at 38.8% of it. The cash-flow path is now a sustain rather than a harvest: capex equals the depreciation charge, so free cash flow to the firm runs from IDR44.2bn in FY2026E through IDR55.3bn, net property and equipment holds at IDR390.4bn, and there is no terminal year in which a depreciation add-back is capitalised for a fleet that has been run down [S5 p.36, F8, F41, F42]. That is the correction that matters, and it is why the DCF is lower than the last version's despite an unchanged revenue path.

The horizon is matched to the contract register, not to a round number. The ten-year mining-service contract for the Wiraduta mine, the multi-year Duta Bara Utama mining and rental contracts and the Medco rentals carry the explicit decade [S5 p.58-60]; the Banyan contract expired on 26 May 2025 and is not in the base revenue path [S4 p.63, S5 p.48]. Value beyond the decade is renewal, not backlog, which is why the terminal growth is nominal escalation only.

The receivable is the item the last version treated one-sidedly, and it is now on both sides of the ledger. The cash flow holds operating working capital at the June 2026 actual and never releases it, so the Banyan balance earns nothing in the FCFF; the bridge therefore credits an expected recovery of seven tenths of the IDR150.3bn balance, collected across the next two years [S5 p.33, F19]. That recovery is a large haircut to the company's own provisioning, which allows a small fraction of the book [S5 p.33, F28]; in its favour are the paydown during the first quarter and an obligor that is an affiliate of the state power group's fuel subholding [S5 p.33, S12, F19, F36]. The credit is applied in every scenario, so the bear understates the loss if collection fails; remove it and the discounted cash flow falls below the market price, which is the honest measure of how much of the call rests on collection [S0].

The capacity the market is not paying for is visible on the free cash flow line. Free cash flow to equity of IDR53.4bn on 3,139.0m shares is a 12.4% yield on today's price, against a modelled distribution of 2.2 a share, or 1.6%, at a 15.0% payout [S0, S5 p.5]. The gap between the two is the dividend capacity the family register has chosen not to distribute while the receivable and the refinancing calendar are open; we treat it as capacity, not income, because the payout policy is the controlling family's decision [S2 p.46].

The cross-checks disagree with each other, which is the honest picture. EV/EBITDA applies a peer median of 5.0 to FY2025A EBITDA - the same year and the same trailing window for every peer - and returns Rp274, or 72.4% above the DCF; the producer-inclusive peer set is deliberate, because the producers own the mine plans and the RKAB quotas that set contractor volumes and rates [S0]. The residual gap is not a mis-set multiple but the difference between a sustaining FCFF and a market that capitalises current EBITDA [S0, S4 p.53, S5 p.36]. P/E applies a median of 6.5 to FY2025A earnings, depressed by a full depreciation charge against a trough revenue base, and returns Rp78, -50.6% relative to the DCF; that gap is an artefact of the trough, not a second opinion on the asset [S0, S5 p.36].

On book, the stock trades at 0.9x FY2025A book and 0.8x our FY2026E book. The FY2026E return on equity - net profit of IDR37.2bn on equity of IDR518.9bn - is far below the 16.0% cost of equity, and a justified P/B of (ROE - g)/(COE - g) at that return is well below one. That is the tension the DCF has to answer: growth does not create value at this return on equity, so the terminal growth is nominal escalation and the value comes from the cash the existing fleet throws off and from collecting the receivable, not from reinvestment. The P/B cross-check is therefore closer to the bear than to the bull, and if the return on equity stayed at the FY2026E level for ever the book value, not the cash flow, would be the binding constraint; the bear case tests a lower margin and growth but not a permanently sub-cost return, which is the honest limit of the model [S0, S5 p.5].

The weighted value before liquidity is Rp196. We then apply the house liquidity discount of 10.0% for a stock trading at IDR1.4bn a day, which brings the value to Rp176; the discount is taken once, outside the multiple, never inside the WACC [S0].

The reverse DCF is worth stating carefully, because the last version overclaimed from it. The engine's solver does not bracket the price, and the reason is mechanical: it rescales the growth inputs, and at its floor it still leaves FY2027E growth positive, so it never tests a contraction [S0]. Rather than infer from a solver that cannot reach the answer, we ran explicit paths. A decade with revenue flat still values the equity above the market price, and so does a no-recovery path in which the quota never normalises; only a path in which revenue shrinks in every single year for the whole forecast falls to the current price [S0, S9]. The market is therefore not pricing a slower recovery: it is pricing a permanent contraction of the fee base on our margins and our cost of capital, or it is pricing the float and the receivable [S0, F16]. Either it knows something about the durability of the client mine plans that the filings do not show, or it is a liquidity and collection discount. The multiple anchors say the same thing: at Rp137 the market pays 3.4x times FY2025A EBITDA on the FY2025A balance-sheet net debt of IDR156.1bn and 0.9x book value, which is a harvest multiple, not a growth multiple [S0].

The sensitivity grid shows the call is not a discount-rate artefact. Across the WACC and terminal-growth band the value moves by less than it does across the revenue and gross-margin band, which is where the two real levers sit: the annual rate reset and the quota. The margin axis is also the cleanest way to show the rate-reset upside the model does not have as a separate driver: a sustained change in the service rate is a direct change in gross margin, and the grid gives the rupiah-per-share value of each point of it. We keep the rate reset in the narrative and the sensitivity rather than as a separate bull shock, because the mirror rule would require an equal and opposite bear shock that the evidence does not support as strongly as the impairment already carried in the bridge [S4 p.53-54, S10, S11].

The first risk is regulatory and it is already live. The 2026 national production plan sits below the 2025 realisation and the RKAB approvals ran late, which is what took first-quarter revenue to IDR57.2bn [S8, S9, F21]. If the 2027 approvals repeat the pattern, the second-half recovery in the base case does not happen. The signpost is the December approval round, not the coal price [S8].

The second risk is client concentration and the dated contract register. Four customers were 88.5% of FY2024 net sales [S4 p.53, F16]. Banyan ended on 26 May 2025 and is now 0.1% of revenue [S4 p.63, S5 p.48, F29]. Budi Gema Gempita, at 45.7% of first-quarter revenue, is inside its renewal, so the FY2026 signature is the event that keeps the base case intact [S5 p.58-60, F30]. Losing that client is the single largest downside in the file, which is why the bear is sized to it rather than to a shave of growth.

The third risk is the receivable, and it is the first thing we would want to be wrong about. IDR197.5bn of the IDR330.0bn gross book was more than three months overdue at 31 March 2026, the allowance is IDR17.9bn, and the three largest balances are Banyan at IDR150.3bn, BGG at IDR79.9bn and Duta Bara Utama at IDR63.5bn [S5 p.33, F19, F28, F34, F35, F38, F39]. Equity is IDR456.8bn, so the balances are material to book value [S5 p.5, F20]. Recovery assumption by client: Banyan at seven tenths on the paydown evidence and the state power group affiliation [S5 p.33, S12, F19, F36]; BGG and Duta Bara at full book, because both are operating mines paying monthly, which is what keeps their balances inside the current bucket rather than the overdue one [S5 p.33, S5 p.58-59]. A ten-point move in the Banyan recovery is the difference between a value above the market price and one around it, so the collection is a monitored number, not a one-off judgement [S0, F19].

The fourth risk is the fleet, now in the base case rather than outside it. A renewal cycle is no longer a surprise: capex equals the charge, hauler availability is already below loader availability, and what remains is the risk that the renewal is bought at a higher price than the charge assumes, which would cut free cash flow further [S2 p.72, F43, F44, S5 p.36].

The fifth risk is refinancing: consumer-financing payables secured on the units at rates in the low teens, falling due mostly in 2027 and 2028, with bank covenants not disclosed in detail [S5 p.5, S5 p.37]. The company has repaid through the cycle rather than rolled, which is the mitigating fact [S0]. The sixth is governance and liquidity together: six family holders, insiders at 85.7%, a float of 10.9% and IDR1.4bn a day, plus the exchange's special monitoring board status discussed in section six, so a value gap of this size can persist for years [S0, S2 p.46].

The base case carries 45.0% and values the equity at Rp186: quotas normalise at the reduced national level, revenue recovers to the FY2025 run-rate, the Budi Gema Gempita renewal is signed, Wiraduta and Medco keep ramping, the Banyan balance is partly collected and capex stays at the charge [S9, S4 p.63, S5 p.36, S5 p.48]. The bear at 30.0% assumes the largest client does not come back at the old scope, the quota stays cut for the whole forecast and the rate reset fails to pass through cost inflation. Because the engine's shocks apply to every forecast year, losing a client worth 45.7% of revenue is entered as a persistent shave of the growth path that removes roughly that client's share of the fee base by the middle of the decade, and the bear value of Rp127 is below the current price [S9, S5 p.59, F30]. That is a different conclusion from the last version, which named a client loss but modelled a revenue shave several times smaller; the red team was right to reject it [S8, S9]. The bull at 25.0% assumes quotas are re-opened toward the pre-cut level, the renewal is signed, a fifth contract is won, the rate reset passes through and the net cash funds a special distribution, for Rp296 [S10, S11, S12]. No Banyan restart is assumed in the bull: a restart would be a new contract win, not a recovery [S4 p.63, S5 p.48, F29].

The signposts that would change our view are, in order: the 2027 RKAB approvals and whether the national target is raised; the Budi Gema Gempita renewal signature and the Banyan receivable balance in the next quarterly filing; hauler availability and the capex-to-depreciation ratio in the FY2026 accounts; and the export-duty regulation and the annual rate reset, which would change the rate clients can pay [S8, S11, S5 p.36, S4 p.63].

The company is family controlled and thinly traded. Six named individual holders held about four fifths of the shares at the end of FY2024, insiders are 85.7% on the market data, the float is 10.9%, and there is no second block that could discipline management [S2 p.46, S0].

The IDX regime check comes first, and the answer is not clean. The exchange placed UNIQ on the special monitoring board on 18 August 2023 under its suspension criterion, after suspending the stock for more than a trading day following a three-month run-up of more than two hundred per cent; the archived record shows no announcement of removal, so we carry the full-call-auction regime as live until an exchange notice says otherwise [S13]. That matters for entry and exit in a name already trading IDR1.4bn a day, and it is part of why the gap can persist [S0, S13]. The price is also down sharply from its high: at Rp137 it sits below the annual high of 498.0 and above the low of 84.0, a drawdown the last version did not discuss, and no corporate action or enforcement explains it in the archived record [S0]. The FY2024 accounts are audited with the usual unmodified opinion and directors' responsibility statement [S4 p.3]; the auditor is Mirawati Sensi Idris, a member of the Moore Global network [S2 p.43]. No accounting irregularity is disclosed, and no notation letter is recorded in the filings we hold.

No share pledge is disclosed, which is the one structure flag we can clear. What the filings do show is a related structure: certain bank facilities are secured by the company's receivables and property and equipment plus a personal guarantee from a shareholder, and several assets of shareholder Jati Simina are pledged as collateral for the short- and long-term bank loans [S4 p.61, S4 p.37]. That ties the controlling family's personal balance sheet to the bank lines and is a structure we would want removed; it is not a margin-call channel on the listed shares [S4 p.61].

Related-party dealings are disclosed and small. Purchases were 2.7% of net sales in FY2024 against about one per cent in FY2023, from PT Kindai Udira Nitya, RM Sederhana Muara Enim and Toko Unit Diesel Utama, companies with the same management as the issuer; there were no sales to related parties [S4 p.54, S4 p.61, F27]. Board and management remuneration is disclosed in the same note and is small against profit, and the FY2024 statements are prepared on a going-concern basis [S4 p.61, S4 p.3]. The dividend record is thin: the last cash dividend was IDR12.5bn, paid in 2024 out of FY2023 profit, and nothing since, so the FY2025 payout ratio is nil [S4 p.13, S0, F25]. The company has preferred to repay debt, which is the right call while the receivable is outstanding and the reason our forecast payout is modest [S5 p.5].

On ESG, the exposures are the ones a coal contractor cannot avoid: the transition risk of the end market, the safety risk of heavy equipment on a mine site, and the rehabilitation liability that sits with the licence holder rather than with the contractor [S4 p.53]. The company reports machine availability and maintenance discipline as its operating KPIs and holds the usual certifications, which is the extent of what the filings disclose [S2 p.72]. We do not claim more than that.

The dated catalysts are the RKAB cycle, the contract register, the price settings and the accounts. The 2027 approvals, expected before the year starts if the miners' association gets its way, are the event that decides whether the revenue recovery in our base case happens [S8]. The Budi Gema Gempita renewal is the contract that keeps the largest client in the base case and the Banyan receivable collection is the cash event, so both belong in the same watch list as the quota [S4 p.63, S5 p.33]. The monthly reference price settings matter for client behaviour rather than for the company's own revenue, and the rate reset at the annual mine plan is where the margin is set; the export-duty regulation now in preparation would change the netback its clients earn [S10, S11]. The audited FY2026 accounts, due by the end of March 2027, will show whether the second-quarter margin held and whether the receivable was collected [S4 p.41, S5 p.33].

Between updates we monitor four numbers: overburden removed and coal produced, because they carry the quota; the trade receivable and the Banyan balance, because they carry the cash; property and equipment additions against depreciation, because they carry the fleet; and net debt, because it carries the refinancing calendar [S2 p.25, S5 p.33, S5 p.36, S5 p.5]. The quarterly filings of the four client mine owners are not public, so the company's own quarterly report is the first place the quota shows up [S5 p.6].

bear.narrative: The largest client is lost. Budi Gema Gempita is 45.7% of Q1 2026 revenue [F30, S5 p.48] and its three-year extension ran out in February 2026 with the renewal still unsigned [S5 p.59]; in this case it does not come back at the old scope, RKAB quotas stay at the reduced national level for the whole forecast [S9], and the annual rate reset fails to pass through cost inflation, taking the gross margin back toward the FY2025 level. The engine's shocks apply to every forecast year, so the loss of the client is entered as a persistent shave of the growth path that removes roughly the client's share of the fee base by the middle of the decade rather than as a single-year step-down (v2 ran -6pp and modelled a 5% revenue event for a 46% client; that was the red team's point and it was right). The receivable is credited at the same recovery in every scenario, so this case understates the loss if the collection also fails.

bull.narrative: Quotas are re-opened toward the pre-cut national level as the government responds to the HBA rally, the BGG renewal is signed on the current scope and a fifth contract is won, the Medco and Wiraduta rental contracts ramp, and the annual rate reset passes through the higher reference price, widening the client-funded margin. The resulting net cash funds a special dividend or buyback. No Banyan restart is assumed: that contract expired on 26 May 2025 and Banyan is 0.12% of Q1 2026 revenue [S4 p.63, S5 p.48]. The bull is the mirror of the bear on the same two drivers: the growth shock is set so that the upside and downside shocks are of similar size, because the quota has been cut and can be restored, and the register contains no single contract win as large as the client the bear removes.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: 1H2026 net sales were Rp212.5bn (Q1 Rp57.20bn [F21, S5 p.6] plus Q2 Rp155.28bn, data pack), against Rp288.2bn in 1H2025, a 26% fall, and Q1 alone was down 58% year on year on the delayed and cut RKAB 2026 approvals [S8] and a national 2026 production plan set below the more than 790Mt produced in 2025 [S9]. FY2026E is set at -13.2% (Rp497bn): the actual first half plus a second half at the first half's average quarterly rate (Rp284.6bn), so the Q1 hole is not repeated and the year cannot recover it. FY2027E is +14.5% (Rp569bn), which is not growth: it holds the FY2026E exit run-rate (the second half's Rp284.6bn annualised, Rp569.2bn) instead of assuming a step-down the filings do not show [S0, S5 p.6]. The Q2 2026 annualised level is higher still (Rp155.3bn times four, about Rp621bn), so the FY2027E line is 8.4% below the exit quarter run-rate; we anchor to the lower of the two run-rates, which is the second-half average rather than the stronger final quarter, and the sensitivity grid prices a four-point swing either way. FY2028E-FY2030E step to +4.0%, +4.0% and +3.5% as quotas normalise at a quota-constrained national output [S9]; this is contract arithmetic on observed quarterly run-rates, not a recovery story: the FY2027E level is still 15% below FY2024.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025 gross margin was 17.66% (net sales Rp572.68bn, cost of sales Rp471.55bn, data pack) and FY2024 was 19.60% [F1, F3, S4 p.12]. The quarterly path is violently uneven because depreciation (Rp26.5bn a quarter [F22]) and salaries (Rp22.2bn in Q1 2026) are fixed against a revenue line that halved: Q1 2026 gross margin was -33.2%, Q2 2026 27.0% on revenue of Rp155.3bn [S5 p.6, data pack]. Half the year is now actual: 1H2026 gross margin was 10.8% (gross profit Rp22.96bn on Rp212.5bn), which is the Q1 collapse and the Q2 recovery added together. The arithmetic the red team asked for, stated plainly: FY2026E revenue of Rp497.1bn is 1H actual of Rp212.5bn plus a 2H at the 1H average quarterly rate of Rp142.3bn, i.e. Rp284.6bn; gross profit of Rp99.4bn at the 20.0% base input less the Rp22.96bn actually earned leaves Rp76.4bn to be earned in the second half, which on Rp284.6bn of revenue is a required 2H gross margin of 26.9%. That is the Q2 2026 actual rate (27.0%) carried forward, not an extrapolation of a spike, but it is 6.2pp above the 2H2025 rate of 20.7% at a similar revenue level, and in a series where Q3 2025 printed 30.7% and Q4 2025 9.6% (data pack). We keep the Q2 actual as the anchor because it is the last observed quarter at run-rate revenue and because the fixed quarterly charge (depreciation Rp26.5bn [F22, S5 p.36] plus salaries) is now spread over a normal revenue base; the requirement is disclosed in section 3 rather than buried in a full-year average, and the gross-margin axis of the sensitivity grid prices each point of miss. At the whole-year level the model's 19.2% against this 20.0% input is the Brent cost link at the live deck (about eight tenths of a point of extra fuel cost), not a transcription difference. FY2027E 19.0% and 18.5% thereafter sit between the FY2024 and FY2025 actuals, so no margin expansion is assumed beyond the observed second quarter. Fuel is Rp149.7bn of FY2024 cost of sales (27.8%) [F23, S4 p.53] and is carried by the Brent link.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Fuel is 27.8% of FY2024 cost of sales (Rp149.73bn of Rp538.79bn) [F23, F3, S4 p.53], but only a fraction of that line behaves like Brent inside a year. The observed record says so: Brent fell 14.7% from FY2024 to FY2025 and the gross margin fell 1.9pp, and Brent rose about 41% from FY2025 into 2026 while the Q2 2026 gross margin was 27.0%, above the FY2025 full-year 17.66% [F1, F3, S4 p.12, S5 p.6]. Indonesian HSD is administered and lagged, and rates are reset in the client's annual mine plan, so the exposure that shows up within a year is a small multiple of the noise in the quarterly margin. We calibrate to those sub-2pp observed swings and expose 5% of COGS, not the full fuel line, which would overstate the cost swing in both directions (the same calibration used for DOID.JK).

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Service rates are set in the annual mine plan with the client and are revised at the next plan, not indexed within the year. The FY2024 accounts show fuel rising 8.6% (Rp137.87bn to Rp149.73bn) while revenue rose 17.3% [F23, F1, S4 p.53], and the 2026 quarters show a 41% Brent increase with the gross margin at a two-year high once revenue returned to run-rate [S5 p.6]. We assume half of any fuel move is recovered within the year and half sits in the margin until the next plan: 50% pass-through.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2024 operating expenses were Rp24.97bn, 3.73% of net sales [S4 p.12]; FY2025 was Rp35.95bn, 6.28% (data pack) on a smaller revenue base, and Q1 2026 was Rp4.72bn, 8.26% of a halved revenue [S5 p.6]. The cost is largely fixed (salaries Rp13.3bn of the FY2024 total, S4 p.54). FY2026E is set at 7.0% (Rp34.8bn, close to the FY2025 cash cost), then 6.0% as revenue recovers, held flat thereafter.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation charged to profit or loss was Rp107.05bn in FY2024 (Rp105.12bn in cost of sales plus Rp1.93bn in opex) [F6, S4 p.41-42] and Rp109.62bn in FY2025 [F8, S5 p.36], 19.1% of FY2025 revenue; Q1 2026 was Rp26.52bn, 46% of that quarter's revenue because revenue collapsed [F22]. The Yahoo D&A line (Rp2.08bn) is only the opex slice and is never used. FY2026E is 21.0% of the lower revenue base (about Rp104bn), easing to 19.0% as revenue recovers; the fleet is not revalued and no life is extended.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capex is now set equal to the depreciation charge in every forecast year, because the fleet cannot be harvested and have its depreciation added back at the same time. The physical anchor is the property and equipment note at 31 December 2025: gross cost Rp996.46bn [F41, S5 p.36], accumulated depreciation Rp606.03bn [F42, S5 p.36], net carrying value Rp390.43bn [S5 p.36], against a FY2025 charge of Rp109.62bn [F8, S5 p.36]. That is 39% of gross cost left, about 3.6 years of charge at the current rate, inside an average depreciable life of about 8.6 years (charge over gross cost less land). A contractor that carries revenue to FY2035E on a seven-hundred-billion-rupiah base has to replace that fleet: replacement capex per year is gross depreciable cost over the average life, which is very close to the charge itself. Holding capex at the recent 11-12% of revenue instead (Rp59.6-70.1bn against D&A of Rp104.4-121.1bn) drove net PP&E to Rp143.9bn by FY2030E, at which point D&A was 87% of net PP&E - an implied remaining fleet life of 1.2 years on a nine-year asset - while the model still added the charge back in EBITDA and the terminal value. The red team was right that the triangle was not physically consistent. Capex therefore runs at 21.0%, 20.0%, 19.5%, 19.0% and 19.0% of revenue from FY2026E, matching D&A year for year, and net PP&E holds at Rp390.4bn through the forecast; the terminal capex is the same 19.0% as terminal D&A, so the terminal value spends what it charges. The observed FY2024-FY2025 spend (Rp87.79bn and Rp63.87bn) is history [F9, F10], not the plan: it is the reason haulage availability fell to 74.2% while loaders stayed at 80.5% [F43, S2 p.72].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Net working capital (receivables plus inventory less payables) was Rp262.4bn at 30 June 2026 on a revenue base that the first-quarter hole has not yet caught up with (data pack), which is 52.8% of the FY2026E revenue; trade receivables alone were Rp312.0bn net at 31 March 2026 [F18, S5 p.4], of which Rp150.3bn is one client, PT Banyan Koalindo Lestari [F19, S5 p.33], a PLN EPI group affiliate [S12], against an expected-credit-loss allowance of Rp17.9bn [F28, S5 p.33]. FY2026E is held at the June 2026 actual in absolute terms (Rp262.4bn, ratio 0.528), so there is no assumed release of the stalled receivable and no positive delta-NWC in the FY2026E free cash flow. The ratio then glides to 0.50 in FY2027E and 0.47 in FY2028E, back toward the FY2025 pack ratio of 44.7%, as revenue recovers and the Banyan balance is collected or provided against; FY2029E onward hold 46%.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The effective rate was 16.4% in FY2024 (tax Rp13.23bn on pre-tax Rp80.83bn) [S4 p.12] and 17.5% in FY2023; the 33.3% FY2025 rate (data pack) is a low pre-tax base with final tax, not a structural step-up. We hold the LK's FY2024 16.4% for every forecast year, which is the rate the accounts show being paid; the difference from the 22% statutory rate is the deductible items and the portion of income under final tax that the filing evidences, and no source shows that regime ending.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest and financial charges were Rp15.56bn on opening debt of Rp169.4bn, 9.2% (data pack); Q1 2026 was Rp3.82bn, about 8.8% annualised [S5 p.6]. Bank facilities and consumer-financing payables are fixed-rate [S4 p.61]. We hold 9.5%.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income was Rp0.18bn on opening cash of Rp24.11bn in FY2024, 0.7%, and Q1 2026 was Rp0.016bn on Rp13.3bn [S4 p.12, S5 p.6]; cash sits in current accounts. Hold 0.7%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Total interest-bearing debt was Rp169.4bn at 31 December 2025 and Rp173.2bn at 31 March 2026 [S5 p.5], with consumer-financing payables of Rp94.4bn rolling as units are replaced [S5 p.5]. We hold net borrowing at zero: the fleet renewal is financed inside the capex line and no new facility is disclosed.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2024 other expenses net were Rp25.56bn, including interest Rp24.78bn, ECL provisioning Rp3.96bn and severance Rp4.49bn, partly offset by a Rp2.34bn asset-sale gain and Rp6.19bn other income [S4 p.12]. The recurring non-interest part is small and volatile; held at zero and left to the bear case.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: UNIQ is a single legal entity with no subsidiaries and no minority interest in the balance sheet (data pack, S4 p.5). Zero.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The last dividend was Rp12.49bn, Rp3.98 a share, paid in 2024 out of FY2023 profit, a 29.4% payout [F25, S4 p.13]; no dividend was paid in FY2025 (data pack dividends paid nil, DPS TTM nil). We hold 15%: positive but below the FY2023 print, because the receivables book is absorbing the cash the dividend would need.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 3,138,983,000 shares issued and paid up at 31 March 2026, unchanged since the 2021 IPO [S5 p.5]; no rights issue or buyback is disclosed. Zero.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR reporting is 4.0%, inside the 5.0% cap. Coal contract mining volumes are quota-bound and the national plan cuts output, so we take the top of the range only because costs and rates escalate together nominally; it is not real growth.

challenges.challenge: The capex/D&A/PP&E triangle is not physically consistent, so the 60%-weighted DCF still harvests a fleet the revenue needs. Capex is held at 11-12% of revenue to FY2030E (Rp59.6-70.1bn) against D&A of Rp104.4-121.1bn, taking net PP&E from Rp390.4bn (FY2025A) to Rp143.9bn (FY2030E); from FY2031E capex is set equal to D&A (Rp124.7-140.3bn) and PP&E is flat at Rp143.9bn. At that point D&A is 87% of net PP&E (FY2031E), an implied remaining fleet life of 1.2 years against a gross-cost life of about nine years (gross Rp978.3bn, FY2025 D&A Rp109.6bn), while revenue grows to Rp738.6bn on that Rp143.9bn fleet - revenue/PP&E rises from 1.47x to 5.13x. The five harvest years therefore carry about Rp45bn a year of FCFF that the capital stock does not support, and the FY2031E sustain step never rebuilds the 63% of the fleet the harvest removed. This is the v1 C1 issue deferred, not fixed: the v1 FATAL was the terminal D&A add-back, and the terminal is now clean, but the harvest years still add back D&A that is not spent. Holding capex at the D&A charge through FY2030E removes roughly Rp60/share from the DCF.
challenges.answer: Capex_pct rebuilt at the D&A charge (21% falling to 19% of revenue) so net PP&E is held at Rp390.4bn, not harvested to Rp143.9bn; D&A is now sourced from F8 with gross cost F41 Rp996.46bn and accumulated F42 Rp606.03bn (39% remaining, 3.6 of 8.6 years). DCF 170.08 to 158.73 and target 180.73 to 176.38, disclosed in the summary [S5 p.36, F41, F42, F8].

challenges.challenge: The report says collection is likely and carries only a 30% Banyan impairment, but the note it cites [S5 p.33] shows Rp197.5bn of the Rp330.0bn gross trade receivables more than 90 days overdue at 31 Mar 2026 (Rp110.6bn at 31 Dec 2025) and only Rp17.9bn (5.4%) of ECL allowance. The Banyan balance doubled from Rp80.3bn at 31 Dec 2024 [S4 p.38] to Rp157.1bn at 31 Dec 2025 after the contract expired on 26 May 2025, and the other large balances (BGG Rp79.9bn, Duta Bara Rp63.5bn) are not tested.
